A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LivingWorld and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Inspection of all 28 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2 supports reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark comparisons, motion-component ablations, runtime measurements, additional in-the-wild results, and a 170-participant human preference study.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, expanded motion analyses, a revised 95-participant preference study, and a new 20-participant interactivity study.

M1.justification: The Eulerian flow predictor, Kabsch alignment with refinement, hash-based motion field, regression objective, and bidirectional propagation with linear opacity blending remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 is retained. The revised overview and named opacity scheduler clarify existing components rather than establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds hands-on evaluation of camera navigation, region selection, and motion guidance with participants from design or software-development backgrounds (Appendix D.7). Environmental-scene and object-motion coverage otherwise remains similar. Increasing the main benchmark from 10 to 60 scenes within retained environmental categories is principally a sample-size change.

E2.justification: PerpetualWonder joins the main quantitative comparison. Both PerpetualWonder and 4DGS-Cinemagraphy join Fig. 4 and the human preference comparison, which previously included only video-generation baselines. The new interactivity study also evaluates a WonderWorld-style baseline interface. Comparator coverage therefore expands across several distinct evaluations.

E3.justification: The main benchmark changes from 10 scenes to 60, balanced across four categories. GPT-4o PhysReal/PhotoReal evaluation is replaced by four VBench metrics and GPT-5.5 PhysReal. The preference study changes from 170 participants evaluating 10 scenes each on two criteria to 95 participants evaluating multiple scenes on four criteria. V2 also introduces distant-pair consistency metrics, hole-rate measurement, and a seven-point interactivity evaluation.

E4.justification: V2 supplements the retained alignment and motion-field ablations with direct global-consistency evaluation over distant points. Appendix D.4 compares linear, exponential, and sigmoid opacity schedules; D.5 quantifies boundary holes, reporting 9.8% for forward-only propagation versus 0.9% for bidirectional propagation. These add direct tests of previously less-supported coherence and rendering-stability properties.

E5.justification: V1's human preference table reports percentages without uncertainty. V2 Table 2 adds explicitly identified 95% confidence intervals, and Table 7 supplies additional ± values whose statistical meaning is unspecified. This introduces uncertainty reporting, but neither version documents repeated training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Main comparison results are replaced under changed conditions: LivingWorld's PhysReal is 0.87 in v1 and 0.655 in v2, which does not establish a same-setting decline. V2 adds VBench results, global cosine scores of 0.91 versus 0.54/0.66 for the alignment alternatives, revised human preferences, and hole-rate and usability results. Existing MCA/FMV values, the supplemental in-the-wild table, and the module-runtime breakdown are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3–C.4 adds mathematical definitions of global cosine similarity and magnitude ratio averaged over distant point pairs, including the ratio's stated range. Existing method equations and local-consistency definitions remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: interactive environmental dynamics from one image, geometry-aware alignment, a hash-based global motion field, bidirectional propagation, and approximately 12-second updates. Localized object-motion integration and the broader future-work scope are also retained.

C2.justification: V2 interprets visual quality more selectively, acknowledging video models' frame-quality advantage while emphasizing temporal quality. It adds explanations of PerpetualWonder's difficulty with diffuse dynamics and nonlinear opacity schedules' loop discontinuities, and acknowledges residual holes and increased interaction complexity. The existing rigid-motion limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 identifies Pexels and Unsplash as image sources and supplies interface controls and questionnaire details in Appendix D.6–D.7 and Figs. 10–12. Appendix B's architecture, normalization, optimizers, learning rates, and iteration counts are retained, as are the GPU and runtime details.

R1.justification: V2 adds VBench and two image-source references and elaborates PerpetualWonder's role as a complementary physics-based comparator. PerpetualWonder was already cited in v1. The broader related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain stable; reference reordering and publication-metadata updates do not introduce additional works.

P1.justification: Section 3 consolidates alignment and field learning under Motion Field Generation, revises several explanations, and standardizes global-motion-field terminology. Experimental prose and appendix navigation are updated, and acknowledgements are added. The introduction, related-work structure, conclusion, and existing implementation appendix remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figs. 2–3 are substantially redrawn, Fig. 4 expands and rearranges the comparator display, and Fig. 7 is revised. Main comparison, alignment, and preference tables are restructured, with the preference results moved into the main text. New benchmark, schedule, questionnaire, interface, hole-rate, and usability displays substantially expand the visual presentation. V1 Figs. 8–10 survive as v2 Figs. 13–15.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method: it complements v1's small GPT-based automatic benchmark with VBench and broader comparisons, directly tests global coherence and boundary coverage, and evaluates actual interface use. Confidence intervals and clearer method diagrams improve assessability. The preference-study population decreases, and Appendix D.2 inconsistently claims to follow the revised main protocol while retaining GPT-4o/PhotoReal results. Despite these limitations, the new evidence addresses important gaps in support for the paper's central claims.
